244.history: The elder of the two ancient mills was the meeting-place of the western pit towns. They gathered first in {{year:VI-0052}} at the widow Sarah Dunmore's kitchen and moved to the pit-shed, and signed there the agreement not to hang their fires on one man's fuel, Ruth Calder writing and the four captains letting her sign for them. When the enforcers came west the town walled its pit-heads with spoil, old Fraser dug a trench across the southern road and let water into it before the frost, and Ruth Calder wrote her letter to the council in Sarah Dunmore's house. After Àth leathan the wounded were carried up the ridge path to her kitchen table. The siege of {{year:VI-0091}} took the six pit-heads one by one while Meikle kept the town's counting of meal and coal; the eastern pit-head was given up without a fight, the last line gave way, Tom Varley went north to Cnoc thais, and Sarah Dunmore opened her own door. Its pits were flooded and capped with the others in the year after the war.
244.known_for: the pit towns' agreement and the siege of the six pit-heads

372.history: The Tuathaich town of the citadel over the holy ford was the fourth of the western pit towns. Its two delegates walked the hill path to Muileann àrsaidh in {{year:VI-0053}}, the elder with a stick in either hand, and signed the agreement in their own hands. Its company of sixty stood at Àth leathan. In the war it opened its road to the regiments without a siege, with Tobar dhearg of the hills, and its pits were flooded; An Clàr Foscailte names no holdouts taken there. A man of Àth naomh went with Tom Varley's six to an Oirthir Ghaothach. Its citadel over the ford, older than any pit, has the town's grain in it now, the pits being capped; the delegates who signed at Muileann àrsaidh were not asked by the regiments what they had signed, and the town has kept the copy of the agreement in the citadel's chest with its charter.
372.known_for: its citadel over the holy ford, and the road opened without a siege

346.history: The small Tuathaich pit town of the western hills was the first of the holdouts and the ground of the first battle of the war. Its pit captain Calder died in the sixteenth year and the hewers kept his daughter Ruth to speak for them; she wrote the letters of the five towns, and was their spokeswoman in Tional nan Tuathach until they walked out. In the war the hewers of the five towns came down to Àth leathan with their pit-lamps lit at noon, and her list at the pit-shed ran past four hundred names in six evenings and near nine hundred souls with their carriers by the battle's eve. The battle of Àth leathan was fought below its spoil-heaps; after it the town's pits were given as flooded. The western seams were capped by the Board's order in {{year:VI-0122}} with An seachdamh rèisimeid standing by, and the regiment built its post on the road below the town. On the field stands the cairn the Tuathaich families built without leave, and it has grown by a stone or two every time the patrols pass it.
346.known_for: Ruth Calder, Blàr Àth leathan and the cairn

269.history: The market town of the two ancient mills had the only pits of the western hills that were reopened. Its pit captain Tom Varley opened again in {{year:VI-0056}} two shafts abandoned since the humans' time; the coal was poor, but it was theirs, and it warmed the town. His hewers found in the second shaft rotted shoring still holding the roof, and left it alone. When the regiments came in the war's first autumn Tom Varley fired his own two shafts with the pits' powder, and the town was taken, forty-one of its people with it; the old widow Mary Kessock stayed at her door and raised a hand to him as he went up the rabbit path to an Oirthir Ghaothach. In the quartered year a hill farm above the town was burned and bread was left on a sill for those in the hills.

408.history: The red well of the western Tuathaich, least of the five holdout towns, had one pit and forty hewers in {{year:VI-0057}}, and sent its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast on a cart that came back with fish. Its stooped captain set his lamp on Ruth Calder's trestle table at Àth leathan before he gave his own name, and his men sang low along their line in the words of An Eaglais before the battle. A boy of the town named Rab was carried up the ridge wounded after it. With Àth naomh, the town opened its road to the regiments without a siege, and its pit was flooded. The coal-for-fish cart has not run since the pit was flooded. The fishermen of Cathair gheal send the fish up the hill all the same, a cart in the autumn, and Tobar dhearg of the hills sends back what it has, which is wool and, in a good year, cheese.

476.history: The Tuathaich town of the white walls against the pirate coast had its fish from Tobar dhearg's coal. Its oldest woman, Annie Drew, gave Ellen Marsh the last telling of An Dealachadh there in the seventeenth year: the smoke of the fires left burning, the new-set boundary stones, and a soldier who gave her mother bread and would not meet her eye. In the war the fleets off the north-west searched its fishing boats on every day they put out; its fishermen petitioned Tional nan Tuathach, folding the petition into a barrel of cod, and the searching went on. The raiders' bays off the town were found empty after the war, and its fishermen say the raiders will return when the fleets go. The white walls against the pirates have been kept whole; in the war the town's women walked them in the evenings to count the fleets' sails, and wrote the counts in a book that went to Ellen Marsh with the rest.
476.known_for: Annie Drew's telling and the searched fishing boats
